scenes.narration: Somebody like Évariste Kimba should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. Following the completion of his studies he worked as a journalist and became editor-in-chief of the Essor du Congo. In 1958, he and a group of Katangese concerned about domination of their province by people from the neighbouring Kasaï region founded the Confederation of Tribal Associations of Katanga (CONAKAT), a regionalist political party.

The life of Évariste Kimba begins far from where the story usually starts. On 30 June 1960, the Congo became independent and shortly thereafter Moise Tshombe declared the secession of the Katanga Province. Kimba played an active role in the separatist state's government as its Minister of Foreign Affairs and participated in numerous talks with the central government aimed at political reconciliation.

Évariste Kimba was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. Following the collapse of the secessionist state in early 1963, Kimba had a falling-out with Tshombe and took up several ministerial posts in the new province of South Katanga. Tshombe was later made Prime Minister of the Congo while Kimba joined the General Association of the Baluba of the Katanga (BALUBAKAT) party.

To understand where Évariste Kimba ended up, start with where Évariste Kimba began. On 13 October 1965 President Joseph Kasa-Vubu dismissed Tshombe and appointed Kimba Prime Minister. Kimba formed a government of national unity and spent the following weeks attempting to achieve rapprochement between the Congo and other African states.

The road from the beginning to the peak of Évariste Kimba ran through years nobody filmed. However, his government failed to obtain a vote of confidence from Parliament, though Kasa-Vubu reappointed Kimba to the premiership in the face of determined opposition from Tshombe's supporters. On 25 November Army Commander-in-Chief Joseph-Désiré Mobutu launched a coup removing both him and Kasa-Vubu from power and assumed control of the presidency.

Each stage of the life of Évariste Kimba made the next stage possible. In May 1966, Mobutu's government accused Kimba of plotting with three other former government ministers to launch a coup. On the 2 June, Kimba was publicly executed in Congo's capital of Léopoldville (present-day Kinshasa) for treason.

The people who knew Évariste Kimba young describe someone already restless. Évariste Kimba was born on 16 July 1926 in the village of Nsaka, Bukama Territory, Katanga Province, Belgian Congo. After receiving a basic primary and middle education Kimba, like his father, worked on the railroad, but continued his studies, taking night classes at St.

What Évariste Kimba built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. Kimba took up journalism in 1954 when he began writing for the Essor du Congo in Élisabethville, a conservative, pro-colonial newspaper which covered Katangese affairs. Later that year he became the publication's editor-in-chief, and held the position until 1960.

By the time Évariste Kimba reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. In 1960 he acted as vice president of the Association of the Congolese Press. The following year he traveled abroad, visiting West Germany, Northern Rhodesia, Southern Rhodesia, Senegal, the United States, Canada, France, Switzerland, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece, Ivory Coast, French Cameroon, French Congo, Chad, and French Madagascar.

The rise of Évariste Kimba was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. In February 1957 Kimba and a group of other young Katangese concerned about domination of their province by people from the neighbouring Kasaï region met to discuss the political future of Katanga. In 1958 they founded the Confédération des associations tribales du Katanga (CONAKAT), a regionalist political party.

Setbacks came early for Évariste Kimba, and the response to them is the real story. In the spring of 1960 Walter Ganshof van der Meersch was appointed the Belgian Minister of African Affairs and sent to the Congo to oversee its transition to independence. On 12 June the Provincial Assembly of Katanga elected him to the Senate on a non-customary CONAKAT list.

The legacy of Évariste Kimba outlived the circumstances that produced it. On 16 June the Katangese provincial government was formed and Kimba was appointed Minister of Commerce and Industry. On 11 July 1960 Katangese Provincial President Moise Tshombe declared the secession of the "State of Katanga".

Few lives travel as far as that of Évariste Kimba, and the distance is the point. This was opposed by the regional Luba-dominated party, the Association Générale des Baluba du Katanga (BALUBAKAT), but Kimba allied himself with Tshombe and maintained that the Katangese Baluba belonged to the Katangese "nation". Dominique Diur also applied for the position, but Kimba was chosen because Godefroid Munongo opposed Diur's nomination.

The childhood of Évariste Kimba contains the adult in small print. In December, Kimba accompanied Tshombe to a conference with leaders of the national Congolese government in Brazzaville to discuss political reconciliation. Though the role of the full Katangese government diminished over time under Tshombe's leadership, Kimba still actively met with Tshombe and held press conferences.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Évariste Kimba — in that order. In April 1961 Kimba and Tshombe went to Coquilhatville for further talks with the central government on political reconciliation and revising the Congolese constitution. Unhappy with the conference, Tshombe attempted to leave on 26 April, but he and Kimba were arrested and imprisoned for six weeks.

The turning point in the life of Évariste Kimba looked like a failure at the time. In exchange for their liberation, the two men signed an agreement with the Congolese government declaring that representatives from Katangese constituencies would appear in the next session of Parliament. In March and May 1962 the Katangese government held further talks with the central government in Léopoldville, the Congolese capital.

Every biography of Évariste Kimba has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. While Tshombe was gone, Kimba went on a tour of Luba areas in Katanga to rally their favour in support of the secession. On 18 May the last round of the Léopoldville negotiations was due to take place, but Tshombe, stalling for time, stayed in Katanga and sent Kimba in his place.

The education of Évariste Kimba happened mostly outside any school. In the aftermath of the secession, Kimba had a falling-out with Tshombe; Kimba preferred reconciliation with the central government, but Tshombe did not wish it at the time. Tshombe went to Paris, while in February 1963 Kimba became Minister of Education of the new province of South Katanga.

What Évariste Kimba wanted at the start and what Évariste Kimba got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. From April until August he served as the province's Minister of Economic Affairs and Minister of Information. In June he went to Léopoldville, to reach an understanding with the central government.

The defining trait of Évariste Kimba was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. In September he attended a conference of moderate political parties in Luluabourg as an observer. On 13 December he was elected president of the central committee of the Entente Muluba, an Élisabethville-based organisation.

Those who met Évariste Kimba at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. That year Tshombe was welcomed back into the country and made Prime Minister at the helm of a transitional government tasked with suppressing a leftist insurrection in the eastern Congo. After this was largely accomplished, general elections took place in 1965 and Tshombe's new coalition organisation, the Convention Nationale Congolaise (CONACO) won a majority of the seats in Parliament.

The private years of Évariste Kimba explain the public decades better than any speech. Kimba also contested in the election for a seat in the Chamber of Deputies, and won on a BALUBAKAT list. Shortly before Parliament was due to reopen, the strength of CONACO faltered, and an anti-Tshombe coalition, the Front Democratique Congolais (FDC), was formed.

The family Évariste Kimba came from matters more than the legends admit. In the months following the elections, the political rivalry between Tshombe and the President of the Congo, Joseph Kasa-Vubu, grew increasingly tense. At the first session of the new Parliament on 13 October 1965, Kasa-Vubu unexpectedly announced that Tshombe's transitional government had fulfilled its purpose.

The first real success of Évariste Kimba arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. He named Kimba the new Prime Minister and tasked him with forming a government of national unity. Kimba had little personal following or national reputation and thus was considered inoffensive to members of Parliament and of little threat to Kasa-Vubu's ambitions.

The last chapter of Évariste Kimba was written long after the fame. Kasa-Vubu also hoped that by appointing another Katangese to the post, he would avoid aggravating persisting secessionist sentiment in Katanga. Kimba's government was installed on 18 October, representing 16 of the 39 political parties with members in Parliament.

The whole life of Évariste Kimba reads like a single decision repeated. Kimba's government was more nationalistic than Tshombe's administration and aimed to curb Western influence in Congolese affairs; it was markedly less amicable towards Belgian interests. The new cabinet sought to improve the Congo's relations with active countries in the Organisation of African Unity including Ethiopia and Ghana, and to distance itself from the members of the African and Malagasy Common Organisation.

Between the birth and the legend of Évariste Kimba lie the years that actually decide it. The government opened negotiations with Congo-Brazzaville, and on 5 November Kimba announced that in its first step towards rehabilitating the Congo's ties with African states his government was renewing ferry traffic across the Congo River between Brazzaville and Léopoldville, which had been suspended for two years. Tshombe's removal from power angered his supporters, and in the following weeks they competed with anti-Tshombe partisans for dominance in Parliament.

The reputation of Évariste Kimba was built in the middle, not at the edges. On 14 November the Kimba Government was presented to the legislature for a formal vote of confidence. It was defeated, 72 to 76 in the Chamber of Deputies and 49 to 58 in the Senate.

Somebody like Évariste Kimba should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. The next day Kasa-Vubu renominated Kimba as Prime Minister, resulting in a political deadlock. On 25 November, Army Commander-in-Chief Joseph-Désiré Mobutu, who had previously supported Kimba, launched a coup removing both him and Kasa-Vubu from power and assumed control of the presidency.

The life of Évariste Kimba begins far from where the story usually starts. In May 1966 Kimba and former government ministers Jérôme Anany, Emmanuel Bamba, and Alexandre Mahamba were arrested by Mobutu's security forces while attending a meeting with military officials. Mobutu's regime accused them of plotting to assassinate Mobutu and Prime Minister Mulamba and overthrow the government.

Évariste Kimba was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. On 30 May the four men were tried before a military tribunal. The trial lasted an hour and a half and the accused were allowed no legal counsel.

To understand where Évariste Kimba ended up, start with where Évariste Kimba began. They pleaded innocence, claiming that they had been working at the behest of officers in the army. After deliberating for seven minutes, the three military judges found the four men guilty of treason and sentenced them to death.

The road from the beginning to the peak of Évariste Kimba ran through years nobody filmed. This was in violation of standing Congolese law, which did not consider plotting a coup to be a capital crime. On 2 June 1966, Kimba and the other men were publicly hanged in Léopoldville before a large crowd.

Each stage of the life of Évariste Kimba made the next stage possible. This was the first public execution in the Congo since the 1930s. Kimba was the first of the four to be executed; it took him 20 minutes to die after being dropped.
